infatuation

in-fach-oo-AY-shun · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Infatuation is an intense but short-lived and foolish passion or attraction.

Her infatuation with the new exchange student faded within a month, once she realized they had nothing in common.

Example

What felt like true love at fourteen was, looking back, obviously just an infatuation -- intense, all-consuming, and gone within a season.

Infatuation is passionate, but it's also shallow and short-lived -- unlike deeper, more lasting affection.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

crush: A crush is a sudden romantic attraction, usually harmless, privately nursed, and quickly outgrown -- the everyday, lightweight word for it. Infatuation is the stronger, more judging term: passion intense enough to cloud judgment, with a built-in hint that it is foolish and will not last.

fixation: A fixation is an unhealthy lock of attention on one person or thing, and it need not be romantic at all -- someone can have a fixation on locked doors or lucky numbers. An infatuation is specifically a passion or attraction: intense, a little foolish, and short-lived.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

disinterest: a lack of interest or personal investment

loathing: a strong feeling of dislike or disgust

Where it sits · how hard the crush grips

liking → infatuation → obsession

liking vs. infatuation: Liking is a mild, ordinary fondness for someone or something -- far gentler than infatuation, which seizes a person with brief, intense, foolish passion.

obsession vs. infatuation: An obsession is an all-consuming, persistent mania, even more intense than infatuation.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: in, into (Latin)

root (uncommon) — fatu-: foolish (related to the rarer English word fatuous, 'silly or foolish') (Latin fatuus)

suffix — -ation: the act, process, or result of (Latin)

Put it together: Infatuation combines in- ('into') with Latin fatuus ('foolish') -- the same root behind the rarer word fatuous -- plus -ation, 'the state or result of.' To be infatuated is, at root, to have been made a little foolish by a sudden, overwhelming attraction.

Use the root in a new word: fatuous: His fatuous excuse -- that the dog had eaten his homework twice in one week -- convinced no one.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Infatuation always carries a hint of foolishness or shallowness -- use it when you want to suggest that someone's passion, however intense, probably won't last.
